26 * Centralising this here keeps the REST controllers thin: they delegate to 27 * {@link #householdId(String, String)} both when deciding whether a new owner shares a 28 * household with an existing one and when deriving the shared household identifier, so the 29 * two always agree on what "the same household" means. 30 *

31 * Two owners belong to the same household when they have the same last name and the same 32 * postcode. The last name is compared case-insensitively after trimming and collapsing runs 33 * of whitespace to a single space, so values that differ only in letter case or in incidental 34 * spacing map to the same household. The household identifier is a pure function of those two 35 * fields, so every owner with the same last name and postcode derives the identical value 36 * automatically without any explicit linking step. 37 */ 38 @Component 39 public class HouseholdNormalizer { 40 41 /** 42 * Derives the deterministic shared identifier for the household with the given last name and 43 * postcode. The identifier is a pure function of the normalized last name and the postcode, so 44 * every owner with the same last name and postcode derives the identical value and it never 45 * changes between calls. It is the first 12 hexadecimal characters of the SHA-256 of 46 * {@code normalizedLastName + '|' + postcode}, hashed via the shared {@link Sha256Hex} helper so 47 * every hash-derived identifier in the app is computed one way. Owners with the same last name 48 * and postcode therefore share the household id automatically. 49 * 50 * @param lastName the owner's last name (may be {@code null}) 51 * @param postcode the owner's postcode (may be {@code null}) 52 * @return the deterministic household identifier 53 */ 54 public String householdId(String lastName, String postcode) { 55 return Sha256Hex.upperHexPrefix(normalizeLastName(lastName) + '|' + (postcode == null ? "" : postcode), 12); 56 } 57 58 /** 59 * Normalizes the last name by trimming, collapsing internal runs of whitespace to a single 60 * space and lower-casing, so households match regardless of case and incidental whitespace 61 * differences. 62 * 63 * @param value the value to normalize (may be {@code null}) 64 * @return the normalized value, or the empty string if the input was {@code null} 65 */ 66 private String normalizeLastName(String value) { 67 if (value == null) { 68 return ""; 69 } 70 return value.trim().replaceAll("\\s+", " ").toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT); 71 } 72 } 73

30 * The canonical form lower-cases the value. Request-level bean validation on the owner DTO has 31 * already guaranteed that any non-null value is a syntactically valid address, so this only 32 * canonicalises; a {@code null} email (email is optional) is left untouched. Because values that 33 * differ only in letter case normalize to the same result, comparing normalized emails reliably 34 * treats them as equal. 35 */ 36 @Component 37 public class EmailNormalizer { 38 39 /** 40 * Normalizes the supplied email to its canonical stored form by lower-casing it. 19	import java.time.LocalDate;
20	
21	/**
22	 * Derives fiscal-year values from calendar dates. The fiscal year starts on 1 July and is
23	 * identified by the calendar year in which it ends, so 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026 is fiscal
24	 * year 2026. A date on or after 1 July therefore belongs to the fiscal year of the next calendar
25	 * year, while a date before 1 July belongs to the fiscal year of its own calendar year.
26	 */
27	public final class FiscalYear {
28	
29	    private FiscalYear() {
30	    }
31	
32	    /**
33	     * Returns the fiscal year (the ending calendar year) that the given date falls in. A date in
34	     * July or later belongs to the following calendar year's fiscal year; an earlier date belongs
35	     * to its own calendar year's fiscal year.
36	     *
37	     * @param date the date to classify (must not be {@code null})
38	     * @return the four-digit fiscal year the date falls in
39	     */
40	    public static int of(LocalDate date) {
41	        return date.getMonthValue() >= 7 ? date.getYear() + 1 : date.getYear();
42	    }
43	
44	    /**
45	     * Returns the fiscal year of the given date formatted {@code 'FY<YY>'}, where YY is the last
46	     * two digits of the fiscal year (e.g. {@code 'FY26'}).
47	     *
48	     * @param date the date to classify (must not be {@code null})
49	     * @return the formatted fiscal-year label
50	     */
51	    public static String label(LocalDate date) {
52	        return String.format("FY%02d", of(date) % 100);
53	    }
54	
55	    /**
56	     * Returns the number of whole fiscal years that have elapsed between the two dates, i.e. the
57	     * difference between the fiscal year of {@code to} and the fiscal year of {@code from}.
58	     *
59	     * @param from the earlier date (must not be {@code null})
60	     * @param to   the later date (must not be {@code null})
61	     * @return the count of elapsed fiscal years (may be zero or negative)
62	     */
63	    public static int elapsed(LocalDate from, LocalDate to) {
64	        return of(to) - of(from);
65	    }
66	}

The build is in exactly its baseline state — my additions compiled cleanly and nothing regressed. Let me confirm the baseline was identical before my changes (one pre-existing failure, one pass) versus now:

- **Before:** `coreRejectsDuplicateIdentity` ✅, `coreIdentityKeyIsSha256Hex` ❌ (identityKey is `+61400000004||11B2B2A3A9A7`)
- **After:** identical — same pass, same failure, same value.

Let me verify `upperHexPrefix` output is truly unchanged (the refactor shares the hex renderer now) — the test log still shows `householdId":"11B2B2A3A9A7"`, confirming it. Done.

## Summary

I did **preparatory** restructuring only — no behaviour change — so the upcoming identity-key redesign lands as small, localized edits instead of complexity piling into the seven flagged methods.

### What I changed

**1. New `Soundex` utility** (`util/Soundex.java`)
The upcoming key uses `soundex(lastName)`, and the soft-match will compare surnames phonetically. I gave that algorithm a clean, dedicated home now, in the exact style of the sibling static utilities (`Sha256Hex`, `FiscalYear`, `LuhnCheckDigit`): a `final` class with a private constructor, a public `encode(String)`, and a private `mapDigit(char)` helper. That's precisely the split flagged as `Soundex::encode` / `Soundex::mapDigit` / `Soundex::Soundex` — so when the change lands, the phonetic logic is already factored out rather than crammed inline.

**2. `Sha256Hex.lowerHex(String)`** (`util/Sha256Hex.java`)
The new key is a full 64-char lowercase hex digest. I added `lowerHex` alongside the existing `upperHexPrefix`, factoring the shared digest→hex rendering into a private `hex(bytes, format)` helper. `upperHexPrefix` produces byte-identical output to before (verified: `householdId` is still `11B2B2A3A9A7`).

With these two seams in place, the eventual edits to `Owner::getIdentityKey`, `OwnerRestControllerV1::createOwner`, and `isPossibleDuplicateOf` become one-liner delegations (`Sha256Hex.lowerHex(... + Soundex.encode(lastName))` / `Soundex.encode(a).equals(Soundex.encode(b))`) rather than places where hashing and phonetic logic accumulate.

### Why I did *not* touch `getIdentityKey`, `createOwner`, `isPossibleDuplicateOf` yet
Every meaningful edit to those methods toward the new design (hashing the key, swapping `householdId`→`soundex`, redefining the soft-match, dropping the household-409) is a **behaviour change** — i.e. the change itself, which I was told not to implement. Structurally they already delegate cleanly to per-concern helpers; the only thing missing was the two utility seams above, which I've now added.

### Test status (important)
The repo's only test file, `AcceptanceTest`, describes the **future v2** behaviour. Its state is unchanged by my work:
- `coreRejectsDuplicateIdentity` ✅ **passes** (and I preserved it exactly).
- `coreIdentityKeyIsSha256Hex` ❌ **fails** — it asserts `identityKey` is 64-hex, which is the *unimplemented* change.

I could not make that second test green without implementing the redesign (making `getIdentityKey` return a hash), which the task explicitly forbids and which would violate "preserve all existing behaviour exactly." So I kept the currently-green test green and left the change's own acceptance test red by design. Nothing regressed relative to the baseline.
